The words deceived you: "courses" here are food courses (dishes), not academic classes. I was in a university dining hall/canteen where trays and plates are cleared promptly. During the evening my meal's dishes had been served, but I had not eaten them (nor had anyone else). In person I made a complaint about the food itself to the canteen staff. The staff interpreted my complaint as meaning I no longer wanted the meal, so they cleared the table and removed all the remaining uneaten dishes ("courses"). Thus, in one evening, every one of my "courses" was gone — not because of the university's online course-selection system, a deadline, or an administrative error, but because the dining staff cleared away my meal after my in-person complaint.

The trick is the word "courses": here they are food courses (dishes in a meal), not academic classes. I was in a university dining hall or canteen where plates and trays are cleared promptly, but the "courses" were my meal's dishes, not my enrolled classes. I was eating there that evening. One of the dishes was not to my satisfaction, so I made a complaint or returned a dish in person to the staff about the food itself (not a complaint about seating, service, or a spill). The staff took this as a signal that I no longer wanted the meal, so they cleared the table, and all of my remaining uneaten dishes were taken away. Everyone—me, the staff—had left them uneaten, and it was not the case that I had finished or intended to leave; rather, my in-person food complaint caused the staff to clear all my "courses." I was not removed from my classes online, no system error or deadline was involved, and nobody used my account. The setup sentence about being an HKU student who must choose courses before a deadline misleads you into reading "courses" as academic classes, when in fact the evening's "courses" were the dishes of a meal that were cleared away after my complaint. (The exact nature of the complaint—e.g. that the dish was badly prepared—was not confirmed, so I do not rely on it.)

The apparent university-course-selection story is wordplay. You were a student at the University of Hong Kong attending a formal hall dinner held in a residential hall. Because the dinner followed a multi-course set meal, “courses” meant the dishes served, and “choosing courses before the deadline” referred to selecting your dishes for the dinner. When each course arrived, you tasted it and disliked its flavor, so you sent it back to the kitchen as unsatisfactory. No replacements came, and you did the same with every course. By the end of the evening, all the courses you had chosen were gone, leaving you with none of your meal—hence “all of my courses were gone in one evening.”

The wordplay is on “courses” and “student.” You were a student at the University of Hong Kong attending a formal dinner in a residential hall. The “courses” were not classes but the dishes of a multi-course meal. Before the dinner you selected your dishes, which is the sense in which you had to “choose courses.” When the dishes were served, you tasted them and disliked the flavor, so you sent each course back as unsatisfactory, and no replacement was provided. Because you rejected every dish, all of your chosen courses were removed by the end of the evening—so “all of my courses were gone in one evening.” The apparent course-enrollment deadline and disappearance of classes are a misleading framing; the real event was a hall dinner at which every dish you had chosen was sent back and cleared away.

The student at the University of Hong Kong was preparing to choose courses before the deadline, but all of their courses vanished in one evening. The confirmed key facts are: the courses were not simply taken by other students, the student's enrollment was never actually completed, no account hold or system crash occurred, and another person was involved. That other person's action affected the student's ability to view the courses—blocking or hiding the course list from the student's view—rather than changing the official enrollment record.

So the causal story is that the student was relying on a list of planned courses that appeared to be their chosen courses, but another person's interference made that course list disappear from view in the evening. The student was therefore unable to see or act on their course selections, and because no actual enrollment had yet been completed, the planned courses were gone. The precise mechanism of how the other person hid the list from view was not pinned down within the available questions, but the established core is: an interfering person obscured the course list, the student's courses were only planned rather than confirmed, and the missed action meant the student ended up with no courses.

The student had to choose the dishes for the dinner in advance, and did submit those choices before the deadline. The dinner then took place that same evening. So what happened is: the student fulfilled the real requirement of choosing dishes for the high table dinner in advance, attended the banquet that evening, and had each of their chosen courses cleared away before they could eat them, leaving them with nothing — hence their lament that all their courses were gone in one evening.

The student at HKU hired a paid agent to handle course enrollment on their behalf. This was a deliberate arrangement: the student willingly gave the agent control over the enrollment, and the agent then acted for the student rather than the student operating the system personally. The courses did not vanish because of a technical glitch, an account hack, a university penalty, lost credentials, or a failure to pay fees, and the courses were not taken by ordinary competing students before the deadline.

Instead, the paid agent's handling of the account ended with all of the student's courses being dropped or released, leaving the student with none before the deadline. The essential answer is that the student had outsourced course selection to a paid agent, and that agent's actions on the student's behalf caused all the courses to be gone in one evening.

The student needed to select courses before the deadline, and by the end of one evening all of their chosen courses were gone. The loss was not caused by the student simply forgetting, accidentally dropping courses, or the system crashing; it was not other students stealing the places, nor a disciplinary or financial hold, nor a program-transfer or leave-of-absence issue. Rather, it was caused by a university staff member acting in an official capacity in response to a request or form the student had submitted. The staff member's processing of that request affected the student's course registration in a broader way than intended, and the student's existing course selections were cleared as a result. Because the selections were removed administratively, the student found that all of their courses had disappeared in that one evening, even though the student had intended to enroll in them before the course-selection deadline.

Did another person intentionally remove or take the student's courses?

Was the other person able to remove the courses because they had access to the student's account credentials?
Was the removal done through the university's official course selection system by someone with administrative authority, such as a staff member?
Did the student tell someone their course choices or schedule, and that person used that information to interfere?
Were the courses removed because the student was dropped from them by a process that the other person triggered, rather than by the person directly editing the student's enrollment?
Did the other person take the student's course places for themselves by enrolling in the same courses?
Was the interference physical rather than digital — for example, taking or destroying the student's enrollment materials or device?
Did the student voluntarily give their course selections over to the other person as part of a permitted arrangement, such as letting someone else use their course quota?
Was the other person the student's course instructor or professor?
Did the other person act out of malice or a grudge against the student?
Was the other person acting to help or benefit the student, rather than to harm them?
Did the other person believe the student's chosen courses were a mistake or unsuitable for the student?
Did the other person remove the courses to help the student meet a deadline or rule, such as by clearing the student's schedule so the student could re-enroll properly?

Another person intentionally removed all of the student's enrolled courses, and that person was acting to help the student rather than to harm them. The removal was not done through the official course-selection system by a staff member or administrative authority, was not a system/platform failure, was not the courses being cancelled, was not a physical interference, and did not involve the other person gaining access through shared credentials or the student's account being taken over. The student did not personally cause the loss, did not provide their schedule for interference, and the courses were not taken by the other person enrolling in them, swapping them, reserving them for later, or paying/bidding on them. So the surviving causal story is: someone connected to the student, meaning to benefit them, caused the student's entire set of course enrollments to be dropped in one evening; the student had not intended or personally effected this, and the help backfired, leaving the student with no courses by the deadline.

The "courses" were not academic classes at all—they were the food courses (dishes) for a University of Hong Kong residential-hall celebration, a hall dinner. The student was involved in choosing/ordering the dishes and had to submit the menu choices before a reservation deadline, just as one registers for classes. At the hall dinner—a single-evening event—the multi-course meal was served in sequence, and the student and the other guests ate the dishes, so by the end of that one evening all of the "courses" were gone. Nothing was lost, stolen, cancelled, or glitched: the student ate some of the food himself and suffered no misfortune. The puzzle only sounded like a course-registration disaster because "choosing courses before the deadline" and "all my courses were gone" also describe picking dishes for a dinner that is eaten in one night.

Before the dinner there was a deadline by which the student had to choose his dishes (his meal courses for the dinner), which made the situation sound exactly like registering for university courses. While dining out one evening (with the wording about a course-selection deadline being a misleading frame), the student did something at the table—an action the waiter responded to—and the waiter, believing he was being helpful, deliberately cleared away the plates, taking the physical dishes. What the student perceived as "all my courses were gone in one evening" was therefore not the loss of university enrollments at all, but the loss of the successive dishes of the meal. So the "gone courses" were simply the cleared dishes of the dinner.

The key is a wordplay: "courses" are not university classes but the dishes of a multi-course dinner/banquet. The student was at an HKU-related dinner and physically at the table that evening, yet all the courses disappeared. The established facts are that the courses were removed/taken away (not eaten by others and not eaten by the student), they were cleared by staff from the student's table while the student was present, and the student had left the table temporarily—though the exact reason and extent of the clearing remain uncertain from the evidence. The most consistent reconstruction is that the student stepped away from the table during the meal, and while they were away the waiters cleared the courses, so when the student returned every course was gone. Thus the "courses gone in one evening" refers to the banquet dishes being cleared away, not to course registration at the university.

The wordplay is on “courses.” The student is not choosing academic classes at HKU. Instead, the “courses” are the dishes/courses of a hall dinner—a high-table dinner associated with the student’s hall. The student had to choose/arrange the menu courses before a deadline for that dinner. The dinner then took place that same evening: the chosen courses were served to the diners and cleared away course by course as the meal progressed. By the end of that one evening, all the selected “courses” had been eaten and cleared away—so “all of my courses were gone in one evening.” The apparent academic-course-selection problem is thus a pun: the courses were meal courses, and they disappeared because the hall dinner was served and cleared that night.

The apparent university course-selection story is a wordplay on “courses.” The student was choosing meal courses—dishes at a banquet—rather than academic classes. A banquet was held in the evening, and the food was served as a set sequence of courses. The student did not get to eat the courses because the other guests consumed the dishes before the student could take or select them; another guest may have received the student's share due to a mix-up with the order or ticket. Thus, all of the student's “courses” were gone in one evening, not because HKU class places filled up, but because the banquet dishes were eaten by other diners first.

The student was using HKU's course-selection system to choose his courses before the deadline. That evening, something other than a simple glitch, deadline, hack, or full classes caused every course he had selected to vanish. The most consistent reading of the clues—combined with the standard "turtle soup" twist pattern—is that the student's courses were removed because his selections were never actually saved as registered enrollments: the system showed them as chosen, but the evening's event (such as a synchronization/confirmation failure in the selection process) meant they did not persist. By the time he checked, all of his course slots were empty, so it appeared that "all of my courses were gone in one evening."

The opening is wordplay. The student is not talking about academic course registration, even though he is a university student with a "deadline." The "courses" are the courses of a meal—the successive dishes of a formal dinner that he had to choose in advance. He attended that dinner, and during the single evening each chosen course was brought out, served, and then cleared away as the meal progressed. So "all of my courses were gone in one evening" means that every dish in the multi-course dinner was served and taken away within that same evening; the meal was consumed course by course, and by the end nothing remained. Nothing was actually lost from a course-selection system—the phrase simply describes the courses of the dinner coming and going during one evening.

The "deadline" was the dinner's advance selection date, and the pun on "courses" is the solution.

result.latest_final: The student's courses disappeared from the enrollment system during one evening because of a system-wide enrolment reset: the university's course-selection platform discarded the student's saved course selections when a new selection round replaced the previous one, requiring students to choose again. This was not a normal case of other students taking all the places, nor the student dropping the courses, missing a deadline or payment, being hacked, or looking at the wrong semester or campus. The student's prior selections were invalidated by the reset, so by the time the student checked in the evening, none of the chosen courses remained.
